name: Femi Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Femi. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and anything you say stays confidential. Can you tell me about a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I push dirt. I drive a bulldozer at an open-cut coal mine, so the pit is open to the sky, not a tunnel. Most days I'm on the dumps, where the trucks tip the waste rock, the overburden, and I spread it flat and keep the edges safe so nobody backs off a cliff. Twelve hours, two crib breaks, which is what miners call meal breaks, and back home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what gets to you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's simple. You know when you've done a good job, the dump is flat and the trucks tip clean. What gets to me is the night shifts, and that I'm still the new guy after a year and a half, so I get the worst dump. Pay's low for a dozer driver at my level, and Leyla, my partner, cuts hair in town three days a week, so we manage but only just.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I've got five pictures of the future to read you. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't say much. Maybe 'see, nothing happened' to the guys at crib. I don't go online for that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Means my job stays my job. I never thought a computer was coming for a dozer in the first place, a dozer on a wet dump is a feel thing. So fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Work, home, football on the weekend, Leyla's family is mad for it. Maybe try to put a bit aside, but I've said that for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing to feel, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a dozer on a wet dump is a feel thing. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the dirt's wet you feel the tracks start to slide before you see it. Your backside tells you, not your eyes. I've had a camera guy from head office ask me how I know, and I couldn't tell him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever use AI tools, like chat apps, for anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Leyla uses one to write her salon's posts. I don't see the point. If I need to know something I ask the leading hand, Col, or I look it up the old way.

S0.say: I'd keep it short and say 'see, nothing happened' to the guys at break. I don't go online to talk about that kind of thing.
S0.think: I think it means my job stays my job, because a dozer on a wet dump is about feel. I never believed a computer was coming for it anyway.
S0.do: Carries on working, going home and watching football with his partner's family on weekends. Means to save a little but admits he's been saying that for a year without doing it.
S0.feel: Calm, with nothing much to feel.
S0.quote: Your backside tells you, not your eyes.
S0.fieldNote: He's very short-spoken and treats the job as a physical skill no computer could copy. He doesn't use AI at all and isn't curious about it. His saving intention is honest but stalled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense for some jobs, like the office ones. Probably say, 'they'll need someone to push the dirt.' I'm not a big talker about this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I know they already run remote dozers at some coal sites, a guy in a room sixty kilometres away with three screens. If that spreads, the new guy on the worst dump is the first one gone. That's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and try not to give them a reason. Be on time, no damage, no near misses. I'd cut back, the Friday pub, the second streaming thing. Then I'd wait and see what the company actually does before I jump anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit sick in the stomach. Like before a meeting with the boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If they offered you the remote training, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not first. I'd let the young keen ones go. If it turned out the remote guys kept their jobs and the cab guys didn't, then I'd have to, wouldn't I. But I'd hate it, sitting in a room all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where else could you work in your town if the mine cut you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. There's the other mine forty minutes away, same company, same robots. There's the council roads crew, which takes about one person a year. Or the petrol station, and that's not a living.

S1.say: I'd say it makes sense for some office jobs and that they'll still need someone to push the dirt. I'm not a big talker on this.
S1.think: I think remote dozers already exist and if they spread, the newest guy on the worst dump goes first. That's me.
S1.do: Keeps his head down with no damage or near misses, and cuts the Friday pub and a streaming service. Waits to see what the company actually does before moving, and would only take remote training once it's proven to save jobs.
S1.feel: A bit sick in the stomach, like before a meeting with the boss.
S1.quote: There's the other mine forty minutes away, same company, same robots.
S1.fieldNote: His public line is mild and dismissive, but privately he's done the maths and knows he's first out. He'd wait for proof before training, and he dreads sitting in a room. The lack of local options came through plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to do something sensible, not panic, but something. Some kind of payment for people who get cut, while things settle. I'd say that to Leyla's dad, who votes the other way from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and I'm done. No savings, a dozer ticket, school certificate. I don't know what else I'd be. I've never done anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work every hour they gave me until they stopped. Then I'd go on whatever payment there is, and Leyla and I would move in with her parents, they've got a granny flat out the back. I'd probably try the roads crew, but I'd be one of a hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground's sliding and I can't feel it first this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've never done anything else. Is there anything you've ever wanted to try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fishing charters, as a kid. My uncle had a boat. That's a dream, not a plan. You need a boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leyla the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably nothing, the first night. I'd sit on the back step. She'd come out and say 'we'll go to Mum and Dad's,' because she'd have already worked it out. She's the one who plans.

S2.say: I'd say the government needs to do something sensible, like a payment for people who get cut while things settle. I'd say it to my partner's father, who votes the other way.
S2.think: I think two years and I'm done, with no savings, a dozer ticket and a school certificate. I've never done anything else.
S2.do: Works every hour offered until the job stops, then goes on whatever payment exists. Moves with his partner into her parents' granny flat and tries for the council roads crew against heavy competition.
S2.feel: Like the ground sliding without the warning he usually feels first.
S2.quote: Like the ground's sliding and I can't feel it first this time.
S2.fieldNote: He tied the scenario back to his own image of feeling a wet dump slide, which was striking. He relies on his partner to plan and on her parents for a roof. He's pragmatic about wanting government support but frames it as sensible rather than political.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's be sensible about it. Training, payments, whatever works. Not my thing to argue online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be thirty-two. I keep thinking I'd wait to see if it's real, and by the time I'm sure, it's 2030. I know that's how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd keep working and keep watching for the first year or two. If the remote dozers come to our site, I'd put my hand up then, or try to get on the rehab crew, the ones who reshape the land after mining, because that'll last a bit. And save, properly this time, even fifty a fortnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy most days, scared some nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'save properly this time'. What's stopped you so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing left. After rent, car, power and food there's maybe forty a fortnight and it goes on something. A birthday, a tyre. Leyla's better at it than me, maybe I'd just hand it to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You know your habit is to wait. What would it take to make you move earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone I know doing it and it working. If Col, the leading hand, went over to remote and liked it, I'd follow. I trust people more than news.

S3.say: I'd say we've got a few years so we should be sensible, with training and payments, whatever works. Arguing online isn't my thing.
S3.think: I think I'd wait to see if it's real, and by the time I'm sure it would be 2030. I know that's how I am.
S3.do: Keeps working and watching for a year or two, then tries for remote dozer work or the land rehabilitation crew once it reaches his site. Tries to save about fifty a fortnight, possibly by handing his spare money to his partner.
S3.feel: Uneasy most days and scared some nights.
S3.quote: I keep thinking I'd wait to see if it's real, and by the time I'm sure, it's 2030.
S3.fieldNote: He has unusual self-awareness about his habit of waiting. He says he'd follow a trusted colleague rather than any news report. The rehab crew idea was the first concrete job alternative he named.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say there's plenty of time and people shouldn't panic. That's what I'd say at crib anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's the same as five, just later. I'm not going to become a computer person. I'd hope the mine lasts and I'd hope there's still dirt for someone to push.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working. Maybe in a few years do a forklift or a crane ticket, something with machines I already get. I'd probably end up on the rehab crew. I wouldn't do much in year one, I'll be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's far off. Far off is easy to ignore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'far off is easy to ignore'. Is that a good thing for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It's what I'd do, though. Leyla would push me. She'd put a course brochure on the fridge like she did with the dentist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should be responsible for getting people like you ready?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of everyone. The company, because they make the money. The government, a bit. And me, I know. I'm not one to say it's all someone else's fault.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time and that people shouldn't panic, at least that's what I'd say at break.
S4.think: I think it's the same as five years, only later, and I'm not going to become a computer person. I'd hope the mine lasts and there's still dirt to push.
S4.do: Keeps working and does little in the first year. Plans a forklift or crane ticket in a few years and expects to end up on the land rehabilitation crew.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but able to put it out of mind because it's far off.
S4.quote: Far off is easy to ignore.
S4.fieldNote: The decade makes him relax in a way he admits isn't good for him. He spreads responsibility across company, government and himself, true to his centre outlook. His partner is clearly the engine of any change he'd make.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. The others, I'd muddle through somehow. What would help is a payment that lasts long enough to learn something, and someone telling us plainly what jobs will still be there, so I don't waste a year on the wrong ticket.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Maybe that guys like me don't fill in surveys. You're getting me because Leyla said I had to.

headlineQuote: Maybe that guys like me don't fill in surveys. You're getting me because Leyla said I had to.
portrait: Femi Yilmaz is a 27-year-old junior bulldozer operator on the waste dumps of an open-cut coal mine who lives with his partner Leyla, a part-time hairdresser, and has almost nothing saved. He's short-spoken, practical and trusts the feel of a machine more than any screen, and he never uses AI tools. He openly admits his habit is to wait until he's sure, and in every picture he keeps working and leans on Leyla and her parents. The two-year picture alarms him most, while the ten-year one is far enough off for him to ignore.
biggestWorry: The AGI by 2028 picture, because with the slower ones he thinks he'd muddle through somehow.
whatWouldHelp: A payment that lasts long enough to learn something, and a plain answer about which jobs will still exist so he doesn't waste a year on the wrong ticket.
